forecasts.label: Interest payable

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Bath and North East Somerset expects £41.938m grant against £46.505m schools deficit
news_drafts.lead:
Bath and North East Somerset Council expects a High Needs Stability Grant of £41.938m from the Department for Education on 30 November 2026. The council's dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, carried a cumulative deficit of £46.505m at the end of 2025/26. The grant follows acceptance of the council's SEND Reform Plan, for special educational needs and disabilities, on 2 October 2026.

The deficit built up through a £13.716m overspend in 2025/26. The quarter 2 monitoring report forecasts a further £19.615m overspend for 2026/27, which the papers attribute to the cost of supporting pupils with special needs, with high needs, the part of school funding for those pupils, the main driver. The papers say the variance is ringfenced and does not affect the General Fund. The performance report counts 2,959 children on Education Health & Care Plans, up 4%, and expects numbers to stay high until national reforms take effect.

The Department has replaced its Safety Valve programme with a Stability Grant to support 90% of the cumulative overspend. The council must hold the money until the statutory override, a temporary government rule keeping such deficits off its main balance sheet, ends on 31 March 2028, and then use it to fund the deficit. The medium-term financial strategy says the council would need to fund the remaining £4.567m from 2028/29.

news_drafts.headline: B&NES expects £41.938m High Needs Stability Grant on 30 November towards a £46.505m schools deficit
news_drafts.lead:
Bath and North East Somerset Council expects to receive a £41.938m High Needs Stability Grant from the Department for Education (DfE) on 30 November 2026. The grant is expected to fund 90% of the council's dedicated schools grant (DSG) deficit at the end of 2025/26, which stood at £46.505m. The council will fund the remaining £4.567m from 2028/29.

The DfE accepted the council's special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) Reform Plan on 2 October 2026, after it was submitted in June. The Stability Grant replaces the Safety Valve programme. The council must hold the grant until the statutory override, a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet, ends on 31 March 2028. It is then to be used against the deficit.

The deficit built up through an in-year DSG overspend of £13.716m in 2025/26, which the papers attribute to a significant increase in children and young people with SEND. The Quarter 2 monitoring report forecasts a further DSG overspend of £19.615m for 2026/27. The report states the DSG variance is ringfenced and does not affect the General Fund. The corporate performance report puts the number of children with Education, Health and Care Plans at 2,959, up 4%. It describes demand as "high but in line with previous patterns" and expects it to stay elevated until national SEND reforms and new DfE legislation take effect.

news_drafts.headline: Bath and North East Somerset schools deficit reaches £46.5m, with government grant expected to cover 90%
news_drafts.lead:
Bath and North East Somerset Council's deficit on the dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) stood at £46.505m at the end of 2025/26, the council's accounts show. The in-year overspend on high needs (funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities) was £13.716m, added to £32.789m carried forward. The Department for Education has announced a High Needs Stability Grant, expected in autumn 2026 once an acceptable plan is provided, to pay 90% of the accumulated deficit. The council anticipates £41.931m, leaving £4.573m for it to fund from 2028/29.

The council's external auditor (an independent check on the accounts) says the deficit grew by 41.8% during the year and is equivalent to about 50% of usable reserves (the part of reserves the council can spend). Its auditor has identified financial sustainability as a risk of significant weakness in each audit year since 2022/23. The council has submitted a reform plan for the grant, and approval is pending. Recovery plans estimate further unmitigated deficits of £17.2m in 2026/27 and £18.8m in 2027/28. The council's own Annual Governance Statement lists the deficit and its Safety Valve Agreement with the Department for Education among two significant issues, alongside service demand and cost pressures.

A statutory override (a temporary government rule keeping such deficits off the main balance sheet) runs to 31 March 2028. The Department for Education will take over the high needs block from April 2028. The auditor's report says that if the deficits are not resolved by that date, they would have to be funded from the council's own reserves.
news_drafts.paper_title: 9z Audit Findings Reports & Audited Statement of Accounts 202526 Appendix 3

findings.headline: The 2025/26 accounts describe the Interim S151 role as held on an interim basis for the financial year.
findings.detail: The Key Management Personnel note was expanded for transparency to clarify the job role undertaken within the 2025/26 financial year. The change was made for information only.
findings.matters: A change or interim arrangement in the section 151 role is a governance fact that finance directors at other councils and lenders reviewing officer continuity will record.
findings.quote: Narrative in the Key Management Personnel Note has been added to clarify the job role undertaken by Jeff Wring as Interim S151 within the 25/26 financial year

findings.headline: The Key Management Personnel disclosure departs from the CIPFA example format, and management has cited disproportionate cost as the reason it was not changed.
findings.detail: Presenting the note in line with the CIPFA illustrative format would require individual IAS 19 assurances for each person. The auditor recorded this as an unadjusted disclosure misstatement with no impact on recognised amounts.
findings.matters: Other pension funds facing the same individual assurance requirement will want to see how the cost trade-off was handled and recorded.
findings.quote: obtaining the individual IAS 19 assurances required to present the disclosure in line with the CIPFA illustrative format would result in disproportionate cost

findings.headline: One Amber recommendation this year relates to Agresso, where a sampled new user was granted system roles beyond their request, with the access removed after the auditor's enquiry.
findings.detail: Management reports the error was human rather than process-driven, with the wrong role selected during user creation. The auditor found no journals posted by the user to Pension Fund codes, and management will consider adding role reviews to its Agresso user audit.
findings.matters: New-user provisioning errors on shared council ledgers that also hold pension fund codes are a control point other councils using Agresso will want to test.
findings.quote: the system roles granted to the new user exceeded those requested and required for the user

findings.headline: The auditor reports three of four prior-year IT recommendations as addressed, with privileged user access on Agresso still in progress.
findings.detail: The addressed items cover Agresso new user access, the Altair service provider assurance report review and IT and cybersecurity policies. Duplicate privileged accounts on the Agresso database remain on the action plan.
findings.matters: Closure of prior-year IT control findings shows the direction of travel, and the open privileged access item is the kind of control councils running shared finance systems will compare.
findings.figures: Three items addressed; one item in progress
findings.quote: IT Audit work this year did not identify any issues in this regard and therefore we consider this recommendation to be addressed.

findings.headline: The Fund transitioned from Brunel to LPPI on 1 April 2026, and the audit reports additional administrative effort from changed arrangements for handling audit queries.
findings.detail: Queries are now sent directly to individual fund managers rather than through Brunel. In some cases the audit used the Fund's access to client portals to obtain capital account statements because of slow fund manager responses.
findings.matters: Pooling transitions change who answers audit queries, and the added workload and slower responses are a practical cost other pool members moving to LPPI will face.
findings.quote: The Fund transitioned from Brunel to LPPI with effect from 1 April 2026.

daily_post.lead: Refund risk is set when agreements are negotiated, so other councils negotiating similar agreements can compare how this council is writing flexibility into them.
